key_claims: Peripheral immune cells were profiled by mass cytometry in 200 participants across distinct age groups, early AD, and exceptional old age without dementia.
ICOS expression across CD4 and CD8 memory T-cells was associated with cerebral Aβ pathology.
In MCI, higher ICOS expression on CD8 memory T-cells strengthened the association between Aβ load and hippocampal atrophy.
Aβ-derived peptides induced proliferative ICOS+CD25+ memory CD4 and CD8 T-cell responses predominantly in Aβ-positive participants in an independent cohort.
Higher PD-1 expression on CD8 effector-memory T-cells was associated with attenuated Aβ-related episodic-memory decline in exceptionally old participants.
PD-1 expression on CD8 effector-memory T-cells was higher in stable MCI than in MCI-to-AD converters.
limitations: The study is observational and does not establish causality.
The sample size is 200 participants, which may limit generalizability.
The study relies on peripheral immune profiling, which may not fully reflect central nervous system immune responses.
The findings are based on specific cohorts and may not apply to broader populations.
what_not_to_say: The study proves that ICOS or PD-1 directly cause changes in Alzheimer's disease progression.
The study provides a treatment or therapeutic intervention for Alzheimer's disease.
The study establishes a definitive biomarker for Alzheimer's disease.
The study includes all possible T-cell states or immune mechanisms relevant to AD.
